tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Financial Literacy – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Financial literacy is the ability to:
options: Understand and use financial knowledge and skills to make informed money decisions
questions.explanation: It covers budgeting, saving, investing and borrowing.

questions.question_text: The OECD/INFE definition of financial literacy is a combination of:
options: Awareness, knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviours needed to make sound financial decisions
questions.explanation: The aim is individual financial wellbeing.

questions.question_text: Financial inclusion differs from financial education in that financial inclusion is:
options: Access to affordable financial services, while financial education is imparting knowledge
questions.explanation: Financial literacy is the resulting ability to use them well.

questions.question_text: An importance of financial literacy is that it:
options: Helps people manage money, avoid debt traps and plan for the future

questions.question_text: Financial literacy protects against frauds by:
options: Helping people recognise scams and unrealistic returns
questions.explanation: Informed people verify offers before investing.

questions.question_text: Financial literacy helps national development by:
options: Increasing savings and investment and supporting financial inclusion

questions.question_text: The components of financial literacy include:
Attitudes and behaviour are important in financial literacy because:
options: Knowledge alone does not ensure good decisions; habits shape outcomes
questions.explanation: Good intentions must lead to action.

questions.question_text: The three basic questions used to test financial literacy concern:
options: Interest compounding, inflation and risk diversification
questions.explanation: They are the "Big Three" of Lusardi and Mitchell.

questions.question_text: The Rule of 72 estimates the number of years to double money as:
Simple interest on Rs 10,000 at 8% for 3 years is:
Compound interest on Rs 10,000 at 10% for 2 years is:
At 6% interest, money doubles in about:
A financial institution is:
options: An organisation that mobilises savings and provides financial services such as loans and investments

questions.question_text: The financial system comprises:
options: Financial institutions, markets, instruments and services

questions.question_text: Financial institutions are classified as:
questions.explanation: Banking institutions accept deposits and offer cheques.

questions.question_text: The types of commercial banks in India include:
options: Public sector, private sector and foreign banks
questions.explanation: SBI is public sector; HDFC Bank is private.

questions.question_text: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are:
options: Banks set up to provide credit and banking services in rural areas
questions.explanation: They were established under the RRB Act, 1976.

questions.question_text: Cooperative banks have _____ tiers:
options: State cooperative, district central cooperative and primary cooperative banks

questions.question_text: Small Finance Banks mainly serve:
options: Small borrowers such as small farmers, micro and small businesses and the unorganised sector

questions.question_text: Payments Banks cannot:
questions.explanation: They accept limited deposits and provide payment services.

questions.question_text: NABARD is the apex institution for:
SIDBI supports _____, and EXIM Bank supports _____:
Examples of NBFCs include:
options: Bajaj Finance, Muthoot Finance and Shriram Finance
questions.explanation: NBFCs lend but do not hold a banking licence.

questions.question_text: NBFCs differ from banks in that NBFCs:
options: Are part of the payment system
Cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques
questions.explanation: They are regulated by the RBI.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Financial Literacy – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: NBFC deposits are not covered by DICGC because:
DICGC insures bank deposits up to:
options: Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank
questions.explanation: It covers savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits.

questions.question_text: Other non-banking financial institutions include:
options: Insurance companies, mutual funds, housing finance companies and Nidhi companies

questions.question_text: A Nidhi company is:
options: A company that accepts deposits from and lends to its members only
questions.explanation: It is regulated under the Companies Act.

questions.question_text: A microfinance institution (MFI):
options: Provides small loans to low-income borrowers

questions.question_text: The regulators of banks, securities, insurance and pension are:
The role of NHB is to:
options: Develop and regulate the housing finance sector
questions.explanation: It is the National Housing Bank.

questions.question_text: Post offices contribute to financial inclusion by:
options: Providing savings, insurance and payment services in remote areas
questions.explanation: India Post Payments Bank has a wide reach.

questions.question_text: Investment is:
options: The commitment of money to assets to earn returns over time
questions.explanation: It seeks future income or appreciation.

questions.question_text: Financial investment differs from real investment in that financial investment is in:
options: Financial assets such as shares and bonds, while real investment is in physical assets like land

questions.question_text: Investment differs from gambling in that investment:
options: Is based on analysis and expected return, while gambling relies on chance

questions.question_text: Speculation differs from investment in that speculation:
options: Seeks short-term gains by taking high risk, while investment is long-term and analytical

questions.question_text: Risk is:
options: The uncertainty that actual returns will differ from expected returns
questions.explanation: Return is the reward for investing.

questions.question_text: The risk–return trade-off states that:
options: Higher expected returns involve higher risk

questions.question_text: Of savings account, equity shares, FD, gold and PPF, the highest risk is:
Types of investment risk include:
options: Market, credit, interest rate, inflation and liquidity risks

questions.question_text: Systematic risk differs from unsystematic risk in that systematic risk:
options: Affects the whole market and cannot be diversified away, while unsystematic is specific and can be diversified

questions.question_text: Liquidity risk is:
options: The risk of being unable to sell an asset quickly without loss
questions.explanation: Real estate has high liquidity risk.

questions.question_text: Interest rate risk is:
options: The risk that changes in interest rates affect the value of investments (e.g., bond prices fall when rates rise)
questions.explanation: Bond prices move inversely to rates.

questions.question_text: A principle of investment is:
questions.explanation: Match investments to goals and risk.

questions.question_text: Diversification means:
options: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk
questions.explanation: "Don't put all eggs in one basket."

questions.question_text: The power of compounding means:
options: Earning interest on both the principal and previously earned interest
questions.explanation: It makes money grow faster over time.

questions.question_text: One should start investing early because:
options: Compounding has more time to work

questions.question_text: Asset allocation is:
options: Dividing investments among asset classes such as equity, debt and gold according to goals and risk
questions.explanation: It is the main driver of returns.

questions.question_text: Tax-efficient investing means:
options: Choosing investments that reduce the tax payable on returns

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Financial Literacy – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Nominal return differs from real return in that the real return is:
questions.explanation: It shows the true gain in purchasing power.

questions.question_text: Nominal return 9% and inflation 5%. The approximate real return is:
Investment avenues in India include:
options: Bank deposits, PPF, mutual funds, shares, gold and real estate
questions.explanation: Each carries different risk and return.

questions.question_text: Sovereign Gold Bonds are:
options: Government securities denominated in grams of gold, issued by the RBI on behalf of the government
questions.explanation: They pay interest and avoid storage issues.

questions.question_text: REITs and InvITs are:
options: Trusts that pool money to invest in real estate and infrastructure and give investors income
questions.explanation: They are traded on stock exchanges.

questions.question_text: Cryptocurrency in India is:
options: Not banned but unregulated as currency; gains on virtual digital assets are taxed at 30% with 1% TDS
questions.explanation: It is not recognised as legal tender.

questions.question_text: Risk profiling is:
options: Assessing an investor's ability and willingness to take risk

questions.question_text: Risk capacity differs from risk tolerance in that risk capacity is:
options: The financial ability to bear loss, while risk tolerance is the psychological willingness

questions.question_text: AI helps in risk profiling by:
options: Analysing data to assess an investor's risk appetite and suggest suitable portfolios

questions.question_text: A robo-advisor is:
options: An automated platform giving investment advice and portfolio management using algorithms

questions.question_text: A benefit of AI in investment profiling is:
A concern with AI in risk profiling is:
options: Bias, data privacy and lack of transparency
questions.explanation: Users may not understand AI decisions.

questions.question_text: Financial planning is:
options: The process of setting financial goals and creating a plan to achieve them
questions.explanation: It covers income, spending, saving and investing.

questions.question_text: The first step of financial planning is:
questions.explanation: Then assess the position, make a plan, implement and review.

questions.question_text: Financial planning is important because it:
options: Helps achieve goals and prepare for emergencies and retirement

questions.question_text: An emergency fund is:
options: Savings kept for unexpected expenses, usually 3 to 6 months' expenses

questions.question_text: A budget is:
options: A plan of expected income and expenditure for a period
A record of past spending only

questions.question_text: A family budget is:
options: An estimate of a household's income and expenses (food, rent, education, savings)

questions.question_text: The 50-30-20 rule suggests:
options: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment
questions.explanation: It is a simple budgeting guide.

questions.question_text: Zero-based budgeting means:
options: Allocating every rupee of income to expenses or savings so that income minus expenses is zero

questions.question_text: A business budget includes:
options: Sales, production, cash and master budgets

questions.question_text: A cash budget is:
options: An estimate of cash receipts and payments over a period

questions.question_text: The national budget is presented under:
options: Article 112 of the Constitution as the annual financial statement

questions.question_text: The Union Budget is presented by:
options: The Finance Minister, usually on 1 February
questions.explanation: It covers the coming financial year.

questions.question_text: Revenue receipts differ from capital receipts in that revenue receipts:
options: Do not create liabilities or reduce assets (e.g., tax revenue), while capital receipts do (e.g., borrowings)
questions.explanation: Capital receipts include loans and asset sales.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Financial Literacy – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Revenue expenditure differs from capital expenditure in that revenue expenditure:
options: Does not create assets (e.g., salaries), while capital expenditure creates assets (e.g., roads)

questions.question_text: A surplus budget is one where:
questions.explanation: A balanced budget has them equal; a deficit has expenditure above receipts.

questions.question_text: Revenue deficit is:
questions.explanation: It shows borrowing used for current spending.

questions.question_text: Fiscal deficit is:
options: Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings

questions.question_text: Primary deficit is:
questions.explanation: It shows borrowing excluding interest burden.

questions.question_text: A fiscal deficit is financed by:
options: Borrowing (market borrowings, treasury bills) and other liabilities

questions.question_text: The FRBM Act:
options: Sets targets for reducing fiscal deficit and ensuring fiscal discipline
questions.explanation: It is the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003.

questions.question_text: Total expenditure Rs 450 lakh crore and receipts excluding borrowing Rs 340 lakh crore give a fiscal deficit of:
Fiscal deficit Rs 16 lakh crore and interest payments Rs 11 lakh crore give a primary deficit of:
AI-driven personal finance apps are:
options: Apps that analyse spending and give personalised advice, e.g., budgeting and investment apps

questions.question_text: AI finance apps categorise expenses by:
options: Analysing transaction data and merchant names using machine learning

questions.question_text: An Account Aggregator is:
options: An RBI-regulated entity that enables secure, consent-based sharing of financial data among institutions

questions.question_text: A risk of using AI finance apps is:
options: Data privacy and security concerns and over-reliance on automated advice

questions.question_text: Financial literacy is needed today because:
options: Financial products and digital services are complex and frauds are increasing

questions.question_text: Financial wellbeing is:
options: A state in which a person can meet obligations, feel secure and make choices that enjoy life
questions.explanation: It is about control and security.

questions.question_text: Financial education contributes to financial wellbeing by:
options: Building knowledge and skills for better money decisions

questions.question_text: NCFE is the:
options: National Centre for Financial Education, which promotes financial literacy (NSFE is the National Strategy for Financial Education)
questions.explanation: It works under the financial sector regulators.

questions.question_text: The RBI's financial literacy initiatives include:
options: Financial literacy centres, awareness campaigns and the "RBI Kehta Hai" campaign
questions.explanation: They reach rural and urban people.

questions.question_text: The "RBI Kehta Hai" campaign is:
options: An RBI public awareness campaign on safe banking, frauds and financial products

questions.question_text: PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY and APY are:
options: Government schemes for bank accounts, life insurance, accident insurance and pension

questions.question_text: AI chatbots help financial literacy awareness by:
options: Answering queries in simple language and at any time

questions.question_text: MuleHunter.AI is:
options: An AI/ML tool developed by the RBI Innovation Hub to detect mule bank accounts used in fraud

questions.question_text: A precaution against online banking fraud is:
options: Never share OTP, PIN or password and use official apps

questions.question_text: A cyber fraud in India should be reported:
options: On the national cybercrime helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in and to the bank

questions.question_text: A limit of AI in financial education is that it:
options: May give inaccurate or biased advice and cannot replace human judgement
